objects.doc: read, write, and edit workspace files
run shell commands in the workspace
the epic/issue board — decompose work into dispatchable issues
durable memories that survive context compaction
show yourself a file, a value, or a function's documentation — the only way material enters your context
fetch a program you already ran, and hand a patched copy back to be run
return your verdict on the work you are reviewing

meta.name: list
meta.doc:
List the functions available on this API object, each with a one-line summary.

Only the functions this run actually bound are returned, so the directory never names a call your program cannot make. Open a view of one function's full signature, argument descriptions and types with `view.open_docs_view`.

session.name: finish

parameters.name: summary
parameters.doc: What you did, in a sentence or two.

session.doc:
End your session, reporting what you did in a sentence or two. This is the only thing that ends it.

It does not stop your program — whatever follows it still runs — so call it last, once the tools have confirmed the work is really done. If your program then fails, the ending is cancelled and you get another turn.

session.name: approve
session.doc:
Accept the work you are reviewing: it meets every completion criterion and stays in scope. This ends your session.

It does not stop your program — whatever follows it still runs — so call it last, once you have actually read the change.

session.name: request_changes

parameters.name: items
parameters.doc: Every change that must be made before the work can be accepted, splatted, one per entry: what is wrong, and what to change. It may not be empty.

session.doc:
Reject the work you are reviewing, listing every change that must be made before it can be accepted.

Each item says what is wrong and what to change; the list may not be empty. This ends your session, and does not stop your program.

views.name: open_file

signatures.signature: open_file(path, offset: nil, limit: nil) -> TextFile or ImageFile

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file to open. Relative to your workspace, or absolute.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.doc: The 1-based line to start at.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.doc: How many lines to show from `offset`.

views.doc:
Read a file AND show it to yourself: you get back exactly what `fs.read_file` returns, and the file also becomes its own item in your context window, attributed to its path and closable by it.

The split from `fs.read_file` is the point — `fs.read_file` gets bytes for your PROGRAM, `view.open_file` shows a file to YOU — so a program that reads forty files to grep them still puts nothing in your window. `offset` and `limit` select a window of lines, and two pages of one file are two views that coexist; re-opening the SAME page replaces what it showed rather than piling up a duplicate. An image file is shown to you as a picture, and is the ONLY way to look at one — `fs.read_file` of an image describes it without showing it.

Pictures are the one thing this call can refuse. Only so many image-carrying views may be open at once (your agent's `imageViewCap`); nothing is opened and nothing is shown when you pass that cap, so close one with `view.close(path)` and try again. Re-opening a picture you already have open replaces it rather than adding one, and is never refused. Text views are never refused by this cap.

Raises `ToolError`: `:limit_exceeded`, naming the cap, when opening a picture would pass your agent's image-view cap.

views.name: open_text

parameters.name: label
parameters.doc: What to file the view under. It is what `view.close` takes, and opening the same label again replaces what it showed. It may not be empty.

parameters.name: body
parameters.doc: What to show yourself. An empty body is allowed: it is how you say that something you were showing is now empty.

parameters.name: label
parameters.doc: What to file the view under. It is what `view.close` takes, and opening the same label again replaces what it showed. It may not be empty.

parameters.name: body
parameters.doc: A block returning what to show yourself.

views.doc:
Show yourself a value your program computed, under `label` — a directory listing, a command's output, a child agent's answer, a table you assembled.

This is what replaced `puts` as the channel into your context: what you print goes to the run's operator, views come back to you on your next turn.

The body may be given as a block, which is what a Ruby program reaches for when the text is built rather than held:

    view.open_text("failing tests") do
      failures.map { |name| "- #{name}" }.join("\n")
    end

Opening the same `label` again replaces what it showed, so a program may refine a view in a loop without piling up a copy per iteration. An empty BODY is allowed, since it is how you say that something you were showing is now empty. Nothing is ever silently truncated.

Raises `ToolError`: `:invalid_argument` for an empty label — a view with no selector could never be closed or attributed — for neither a `body` argument nor a block, and `:limit_exceeded`, naming the cap, for a body or label over gg's caps.

views.name: open_docs_view

parameters.name: target
parameters.doc: The function to document — its name, or the method itself.

views.doc:
Show yourself the full documentation for one function: its signature, its description, and the declarations of any types it refers to that you have not already been shown this session.

Name it with a Symbol (`view.open_docs_view(:read_file)`), with a String, or with the method itself (`view.open_docs_view(fs.method(:read_file))`).

This is how you read what a function does. It is a **view**, not a return value — the documentation arrives in your next prompt under a `Documentation` heading keyed by the function name, exactly as a file or a computed value arrives — so it is not available in the turn you ask for it. Plan for that: ask in one turn, use it in the next. Opening the same function's docs again replaces the view rather than adding a second copy, and `view.close(name)` closes it when you are done with it. `<object>.list` is how you find out which names exist.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` for an unknown or unbound name.

views.name: close

parameters.name: selector
parameters.doc: What the view is filed under: a file's path, a text view's label, or a documentation view's function name.

views.doc:
Close every view carrying `selector` — for a file that is every page of that path, for a text view the one with that label, for a documentation view the function's name — and return how many were closed, freeing the tokens they occupied.

Closing a selector that is not open returns `0` rather than failing, so a program that tidies up unconditionally does not have to guard every call. Closing a file view forgets what you read, not what exists; closing a text view discards the only copy of what it held, so write anything you will need later to a file or a memory first.

views.name: current
views.doc:
List what is open in your context window right now: each view's `kind`, the `selector` that closes it, roughly what it costs you in `tokens`, and — for a paged file view — the `region` it covers.

It is called `current` rather than `list` because every API object already carries a `list` that lists that object's own functions. Read it before deciding what to close when your window is filling up.

programs.name: history
programs.doc:
The programs you have already run this session, oldest first — each with the turn it ran on, how big it was, and whether it ran to its end.

It lists shapes, not sources: fetch the one you want with `programs.get(turn)`. The list survives a compaction, so it is also how you find a program whose text has left your context window. It is empty — never an error — for a session that has run nothing yet.

programs.name: get

parameters.name: turn
parameters.doc: The turn whose program to fetch, as `programs.history` reports it. Leave it out for your most recent one.

programs.doc:
The exact source of one program you ran, as a string. With no argument, your most recent one.

This is the first half of fixing a program without rewriting it: get what ran, patch it with ordinary string work (`sub`, an interpolation, a regexp), and hand the result to `programs.rerun`. What comes back is the program that **executed** — so when a turn's program was itself handed over by `programs.rerun`, you get the program that ran, not the few lines that asked for it, and fetch-patch-run composes turn after turn.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found`, naming the turns that are held, for a turn that ran no program or one old enough that the library has dropped it.

programs.name: rerun

parameters.name: source
parameters.doc: The program to run in place of this one. It may not be blank.

programs.doc:
Hand gg a program to run in place of this one. Your program finishes, then gg runs `source` as this turn's program.

Use it with `programs.get` to fix a program without re-emitting it. Nothing is undone: every call your program already made stands, and the program that runs next sees the world your program left behind — so hand over BEFORE doing work you do not want done twice.

The first call stands. If your program then raises, the hand-over is cancelled along with everything else the failed program decided, and you get an ordinary error turn instead. Chains are bounded: hand over once per turn, and write the fixed program to do the work.

Raises `ToolError`: `:refused` for a second hand-over in one turn — a silently replaced program is a change you cannot see — and `:invalid_argument` for a blank source.

tools.name: shell

parameters.name: command
parameters.doc: The command line, run by `sh -c` with your workspace as its working directory.

parameters.name: timeout_secs
parameters.doc: How long to let it run before killing it. Leave it out for gg's own default of 120 seconds, which is clamped to whatever is left of the run's wall-clock budget.

tools.doc:
Run a command with `sh -c` in the workspace directory and return its merged stdout and stderr.

A non-zero exit is NOT a failure — check `exit_code` on the result; only a process that could not be launched, or one the timeout killed, raises. `timeout_secs` defaults to 120 seconds and is clamped to whatever is left of the run's wall-clock budget.

This run may **offload** shell output — the `shell` tool's own description says which mode is in force. Under `offload`, `output` holds only the tail that fits and ends with a note naming the two files the command's full stdout and stderr were written to. Under `adaptive` (the default), a command that **succeeded** returns no output at all, only that note; one that **failed** returns the tail. Grep the named files instead of re-running the command.

tools.name: read_file

signatures.signature: read_file(path, offset: nil, limit: nil) -> TextFile or ImageFile

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file to read. Relative to your workspace, or absolute for anything else in this container.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.doc: The 1-based line to start at. Honoured only under a capped read policy.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.doc: How many lines to return from `offset`. Honoured only under a capped read policy.

tools.doc:
Read a file, returning a `TextFile` or an `ImageFile` — the format is detected from the file's bytes, never its extension.

This gets bytes for your PROGRAM and puts NOTHING in your context window; `view.open_file` is the call that shows the file to you. A relative path resolves against your workspace; an absolute one is read as given, so anything in this container — an offloaded command's output under `/tmp/gg-shell`, say — is readable.

Reading an IMAGE describes it to your program — label, media type, byte size — and does not show it to YOU: the pixels reach neither your program nor your context window, so a file you only `read_file` is a file you have not looked at. `view.open_file` is the one way to actually see a picture.

Narrow the two with an ordinary `case`:

    case fs.read_file("logo.png")
    when TextFile then …
    when ImageFile then …
    end

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` for a missing path.

tools.name: write_file

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: Where to write. Relative to your workspace, or absolute. Parent directories are created for you.

parameters.name: contents
parameters.doc: The UTF-8 text to write. It replaces the file entirely.

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: Where to write. Relative to your workspace, or absolute. Parent directories are created for you.

parameters.name: contents
parameters.doc: A block returning the UTF-8 text to write. It replaces the file entirely.

tools.doc:
Write UTF-8 text to a file, creating parent directories and replacing any existing file, and return the number of bytes written.

Writing is the expensive direction of the sandbox — rewriting more than a few dozen large files in one program exhausts its fuel budget, so split a large rewrite across several turns.

The contents may be given as a block, which is what a Ruby program reaches for when the text is assembled rather than held: `fs.write_file("notes.md") { rows.join("\n") }`.

Raises `ToolError`: `:invalid_argument` when neither a `contents` argument nor a block was given.

tools.name: edit_file

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file to edit.

parameters.name: old_string
parameters.doc: The exact text to find, including its whitespace. It must appear exactly once.

parameters.name: new_string
parameters.doc: The text to put in its place. An empty string deletes the match.

tools.doc:
Replace the one exact occurrence of `old_string` in a file with `new_string`.

Widen the surrounding context until the match is unique rather than counting occurrences.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` when the text does not appear, and `:conflict` — with the number of matches — when it appears more than once.

tools.name: list_dir

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The directory to list; leave it out for your workspace root.

tools.doc:
List a directory, sorted by name; defaults to your workspace.

Each entry carries a bare `name` — join it with the directory you listed — and its `kind`. An empty directory is an empty array, not a failure.

tools.name: read_skill

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The skill's name, as the system prompt lists it.

tools.doc:
Read a skill by name and return its body with the front matter stripped; reading it also pins that body permanently into your context, so a skill you have read stays read.

A skill may be **code** rather than prose, or as well as it. If it carries code, reading it binds that code at `lib.<key>` for the rest of your session and the reply names the key and what it offers. If it carries an on-use script, gg runs it once your program has ended, and whatever it shows you arrives on your next turn.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found`, listing the skills that do exist, when the name is unknown.

tools.name: write_memory

signatures.signature: write_memory(name, description, body, code: nil, on_use: nil) -> MemoryUsage

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The memory's slug: letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`. It is what every other memory call takes, and no two memories may share one.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: A one-line description of what the memory holds. Where the run keeps a memory index this is the memory's line in it, and so all you see of the memory until you read it.

parameters.name: body
parameters.doc: The memory's contents.

parameters.name: code
parameters.doc: A Ruby module whose methods are bound at `lib.<name>` for the rest of your session. Leave it out for a memory that is only prose.

parameters.name: on_use
parameters.doc: A script gg runs the first time the memory comes into use; whatever it shows you arrives on your next turn. Leave it out for a memory that runs nothing.

tools.doc:
Record a durable memory that survives context compaction, and return how much of the memory budget is now used.

A memory may also carry **code**. `code` is a Ruby module whose methods are bound at `lib.<name>` in every later program you write, so a helper you get right once you never write again; `on_use` is a script gg runs the first time the memory comes into use, whose views reach you on your next turn. Neither is context — they cost you no window, are never shown back to you, and count against no body limit — and both are bounded on their own.

Raises `ToolError`: `:conflict` on a duplicate name, and `:limit_exceeded` when the body would breach the run's caps — revise or delete a memory rather than accruing more.

tools.name: update_memory

signatures.signature: update_memory(name, description, body, code: nil, on_use: nil) -> MemoryUsage

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The slug of the memory to replace. Every other argument replaces what it held.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: The one-line description to replace the old one with.

parameters.name: body
parameters.doc: The contents to replace the old ones with.

parameters.name: code
parameters.doc: The Ruby module to replace the old one with. Leave it out to clear it.

parameters.name: on_use
parameters.doc: The script to replace the old one with. Leave it out to clear it.

tools.doc:
Replace an existing memory's description and body, keyed on its `name`, and return the memory budget.

Its `code` and `on_use` are replaced too — leaving them out clears them.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` when no memory has that name.

tools.name: create_memory

signatures.signature: create_memory(name, description, body, code: nil, on_use: nil) -> MemoryUsage

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The memory's slug: letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`. No two memories may share one.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: A one-line description of what the memory holds. Required where the run keeps an index, since that is the memory's line in it.

parameters.name: body
parameters.doc: The initial contents. They stay out of your context window until you read them.

parameters.name: code
parameters.doc: A Ruby module bound at `lib.<name>` once you read the memory. Leave it out for a memory that is only prose.

parameters.name: on_use
parameters.doc: A script gg runs on that first read. Leave it out for a memory that runs nothing.

tools.doc:
Record a new memory whose contents are kept OUT of your context window until you read them, and return the memory budget.

Raises `ToolError`: `:conflict` on a duplicate slug, and `:limit_exceeded` when the contents, or the index entry, would breach a limit.

tools.name: read_memory

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The memory's slug.

tools.doc:
Read one memory's full contents, by slug — the only thing that brings them into your context.

If the memory carries code, reading it also loads that code: the reply names the `lib.<key>` it is bound at, and it stays bound for the rest of your session.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` when no memory has that slug.

tools.name: edit_memory

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The slug of the memory to revise.

parameters.name: search
parameters.doc: The exact text to find in its contents. It must appear exactly once.

parameters.name: replace
parameters.doc: The text to put in its place.

tools.doc:
Revise a memory in place by replacing the one exact occurrence of `search` with `replace`, and return the memory budget.

Append by quoting the last line and replacing it with itself plus what you are adding.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` when the text does not appear, `:conflict` when it appears more than once, `:limit_exceeded` when the result would be too long, and `:invalid_argument` when the edit would leave the memory empty — delete it instead.

tools.name: search_memories

parameters.name: keywords
parameters.doc: The words to look for, splatted. Several specific words rank better than one sentence, because a memory is ranked by how many of them it mentions.

tools.doc:
Find the memories mentioning any of `keywords`, best first: plain case-insensitive substring matching over each memory's slug, description and contents, ranked by how many of your keywords a memory mentions and then by how often.

Pass several specific words rather than one sentence, then `read_memory` the hits worth having in full. A search that matches nothing is an empty array.

Raises `ToolError`: `:invalid_argument` when every keyword is empty.

tools.name: delete_memory

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The memory's slug.

tools.doc:
Evict a memory by name, freeing room in the budget, and return what is left in use.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` when no memory has that name.

tools.name: add_task

signatures.signature: add_task(id, title, description: nil, blocked_by: []) -> TaskUsage

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The id you choose for it. It is what every other task call takes, and no two tasks may share one.

parameters.name: title
parameters.doc: A short line naming the work.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: What the work is, at whatever length is useful.

parameters.name: blocked_by
parameters.doc: The ids of the tasks that must be done before this one. Defaults to none.

tools.doc:
Add a task to the task DAG and return the task budget.

Raises `ToolError`: `:conflict` on a duplicate id or on an edge that would close a cycle.

tools.name: update_task

signatures.signature: update_task(id, title: nil, description: UNCHANGED, status: nil) -> nil

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The task to revise.

parameters.name: title
parameters.doc: The title to replace the old one with. Leave it out to keep the one it has.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: The description to replace the old one with; `nil` clears it, and leaving it out (or passing `UNCHANGED`) keeps the one it has.

parameters.name: status
parameters.doc: Where the task now stands — one of `TaskStatus`'s symbols. Leave it out to keep the status it has.

tools.doc:
Revise a task's title, description and/or status; supply at least one.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` for an unknown id.

tools.name: set_blocked_by

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The task whose blockers to replace.

parameters.name: blocked_by
parameters.doc: The ids of every task that must now be done before it, splatted. Passing none clears them all.

tools.doc:
Replace a task's whole blocker set; no arguments clears every blocker.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` for an unknown id, and `:conflict` when an edge would close a cycle.

tools.name: complete_task

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The task to mark done.

tools.doc:
Mark a task done.

Tasks it was blocking become actionable once every one of their blockers is done.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` for an unknown id.

tools.name: remove_task

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The task to remove.

tools.doc:
Remove a task and every blocker edge pointing at it, and return the task budget.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` for an unknown id.

tools.name: create_epic

parameters.name: prefix
parameters.doc: 3-6 letters naming it. Upper-cased, it becomes the epic's id and the stem its issues are numbered from.

parameters.name: title
parameters.doc: A short line naming the body of work.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: What the epic covers, for a reader who has not seen its issues.

tools.doc:
Create an epic to group related issues, and return the id it took and the board budget.

`prefix` is upper-cased and becomes the epic's id, which is also what its issues are numbered from — a prefix of `auth` gives issues `AUTH-1`, `AUTH-2`, and so on.

Raises `ToolError`: `:invalid_argument` when the prefix is not 3-6 letters, and `:conflict` when another epic already holds it.

tools.name: create_issue

signatures.signature: create_issue(title, in_scope, out_of_scope, completion_criteria, agent, description: nil, blocked_by: [], epic_id: nil, reviewers: []) -> IssueCreated

parameters.name: title
parameters.doc: A short line naming the work.

parameters.name: in_scope
parameters.doc: What the issue covers, precisely. Part of the brief a child agent is given.

parameters.name: out_of_scope
parameters.doc: What the issue deliberately does not cover, so the work stops where you meant it to.

parameters.name: completion_criteria
parameters.doc: What must be true for the issue to be done. It is what a reviewer checks the work against.

parameters.name: agent
parameters.doc: The agent the issue is dispatched to. It must be one you may spawn.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: What the work is. Written for a child agent with no other context.

parameters.name: blocked_by
parameters.doc: The ids of every issue that must be done before this one. Defaults to none.

parameters.name: epic_id
parameters.doc: The id of an existing epic to group it under. Leave it out to leave it ungrouped and numbered under `ISSUE`.

parameters.name: reviewers
parameters.doc: The agents that must approve the work, from the same set you may spawn. Required when this run's reviewers feature is on.

tools.doc:
Create a self-contained, dispatchable issue, and return the id the board **assigned** it.

The id is numbered under its epic's prefix (`AUTH-1`, `AUTH-2`, …), or under `ISSUE` when it has no epic; you do not choose it, so keep the returned one to block a later issue on this one or to wait for it. `in_scope`, `out_of_scope` and `completion_criteria` are what a child agent is briefed from, so write them for a reader with no other context.

Raises `ToolError`: `:invalid_argument` when `agent` or a reviewer is not yours to assign, and `:conflict` on a blocker edge that would close a cycle.

tools.name: update_issue

signatures.signature: update_issue(id, title: nil, description: UNCHANGED, in_scope: nil, out_of_scope: nil, completion_criteria: nil, status: nil, epic_id: UNCHANGED) -> nil

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The issue to revise.

parameters.name: title
parameters.doc: The title to replace the old one with. Leave it out to keep the one it has.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: The description to replace the old one with; `nil` clears it, and leaving it out (or passing `UNCHANGED`) keeps the one it has.

parameters.name: in_scope
parameters.doc: The scope statement to replace the old one with.

parameters.name: out_of_scope
parameters.doc: The non-scope statement to replace the old one with.

parameters.name: completion_criteria
parameters.doc: The completion criteria to replace the old ones with.

parameters.name: status
parameters.doc: Where the issue now stands — one of `IssueStatus`'s symbols. Leave it out to keep the status it has.

parameters.name: epic_id
parameters.doc: The epic to regroup it under; `nil` detaches it from the one it has, and leaving it out (or passing `UNCHANGED`) keeps the grouping.

tools.doc:
Revise an issue; supply at least one field.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` for an unknown id.

tools.name: set_issue_blocked_by

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The issue whose blockers to replace.

parameters.name: blocked_by
parameters.doc: The ids of every issue that must now be done before it, splatted. Passing none clears them all.

tools.doc:
Replace an issue's whole blocker set; no arguments clears every blocker.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` for an unknown id, and `:conflict` when an edge would close a cycle.

tools.name: remove_epic

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The epic to remove.

tools.doc:
Remove an epic, keeping its issues and ungrouping them, and return the board budget.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` for an unknown id.

tools.name: remove_issue

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The issue to remove.

tools.doc:
Remove an issue and every blocker edge pointing at it, and return the board budget.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` for an unknown id.

tools.name: wait_for_issue

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The issue to wait on. It may not be the issue you were assigned to implement.

tools.doc:
Register a wait on an issue and return an acknowledgement.

It does not block inside your program — it records the wait and returns at once, so the rest of your program still runs; the suspension happens after the program ends, between turns. Once the program finishes the run suspends, freeing this agent's slot for others, until the issue is terminal (done, or failed if its assigned agent could not complete it), then resumes on the next turn. Use it to sequence your next turn's work behind an issue you depend on.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` for an unknown id.

tools.name: evict_file_view

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file whose views to drop. Leave it out to drop every file view you hold.

tools.doc:
Drop the contents of files you have read out of your context window, freeing the tokens they occupy, and report what that reclaimed.

The files on disk are untouched — this forgets what you read, not what exists.

tools.name: archive_thread

parameters.name: ranges
parameters.doc: The inclusive spans of turn numbers to move out of your window, splatted: `context.archive_thread(4..19, 30..35)`.

tools.doc:
Move whole turns out of your context window and report what that reclaimed.

Every result you are given carries a header with its turn number and roughly what holding it costs, so name the turns worth dropping: `context.archive_thread(4..19)` archives turns 4 through 19, both ends included. Your own messages in an archived turn are dropped; the results are kept and stay searchable with `context.search_archive`.

Raises `ToolError`: `:invalid_argument` for anything that is not a range of turn numbers.

tools.name: search_archive

parameters.name: query
parameters.doc: The substring to look for. Matching is case-insensitive.

tools.doc:
Search archived history for a case-insensitive substring, most recent first, up to 8 hits.

Check `archive_empty?` before reading `hits`: it distinguishes "nothing has been archived yet" from "the search ran and matched nothing", so you do not archive again believing the first archive failed.

tools.name: compact

parameters.name: summary
parameters.doc: What your restarted window opens with. Write it for your future self: everything not in it and not re-read from `files` is gone.

parameters.name: files
parameters.doc: The paths to read afresh into the restarted window. Defaults to none.

tools.doc:
Compact your context window: the detailed thread is dropped and restarted from `summary`, plus a fresh read of each path in `files`.

Your skills, memories and task list are kept as they are. You are asked to call this when your window is full, and every other call is refused until you do.

It does NOT stop your program: it registers the request and returns, and the rewrite happens once your program has ended. Everything not in your summary and not in `files` is gone, so write the summary for your future self and name the files you will actually need in hand.

tools.name: spawn_subagent

signatures.signature: spawn_subagent(agent, prompt: nil, issue_id: nil) -> SubagentHandle

parameters.name: agent
parameters.doc: The agent profile to run the child as, from the ones you may spawn — the system prompt lists them. It selects the child's model, tools and instructions.

parameters.name: prompt
parameters.doc: Self-contained instructions for the child. Give this or `issue_id`, never both and never neither.

parameters.name: issue_id
parameters.doc: The board issue to brief the child from. Give this or `prompt`, never both and never neither.

tools.doc:
Delegate scoped work to a child agent and return its handle immediately — the child runs in parallel while your program continues.

Brief it with exactly one of `prompt` (self-contained instructions) or `issue_id` (a board issue). The child shares your workspace.

Raises `ToolError`: `:limit_exceeded` at the delegation depth cap, and `:invalid_argument` if `agent` is not one you may spawn.

tools.name: wait_for_subagents

parameters.name: ids
parameters.doc: The children to wait for, splatted. Pass none to wait for every one still outstanding.

tools.doc:
Block until the named children have finished — or, with no arguments, until every outstanding child has — and collect their results in dispatch order.

The run's wall-clock budget keeps running while you wait, so wait once for many children rather than once per child.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` for an unknown id.

tools.name: send_message

parameters.name: agent_id
parameters.doc: The child to deliver to, as `spawn_subagent` returned it.

parameters.name: message
parameters.doc: What to put in its inbox. It reads it at its next turn.

tools.doc:
Deliver a message to a running child agent's inbox; it reads the message at its next turn.

Raises `ToolError`: `:not_found` for an unknown agent id, and `:conflict` when that child has already returned.

tools.name: transition_state

parameters.name: state
parameters.doc: The state to move on to, named the way you name an agent to spawn.

parameters.name: note
parameters.doc: The opening message the next state's agent sees.

tools.doc:
Move the process you are running inside on to another of its states, naming the state the way you name an agent to spawn.

Bound only when a state machine is driving you and the state you are in has somewhere to go. Like `context.compact` it is registered rather than performed: the call validates the target, returns, and your program runs on to its end — the transition happens after that, because replacing your agent (and your window) mid-program would pull every remaining call out from under it. The FIRST declaration stands.

Raises `ToolError`: `:refused` for a second declaration in one turn, and `:invalid_argument` for a state you may not move to.

tools.name: exec

parameters.name: agent
parameters.doc: The agent to become, from the ones you may become.

parameters.name: prompt
parameters.doc: Its opening message. It already has your whole conversation, so this is the instruction rather than a briefing.

tools.doc:
Continue this session as a different agent: the named agent takes over from your next turn with its own model, tools and instructions, keeping every capability the two of you both have — your whole conversation above all, so it needs no catching up.

Registered rather than performed, exactly as `transition_state` is and for the same reason: your window would otherwise be pulled out from under the program still composing into it. A session makes one succession per turn. Bound only when your agent may make agent transitions and has agents it may become, and never while a state machine is driving you.

Raises `ToolError`: `:refused` for an `exec` after a `transition_state` or a second `exec`, and `:invalid_argument` for an agent you may not become.

tools.name: fork

parameters.name: prompt
parameters.doc: What the copy is to do instead of what you are doing. It has your whole conversation already, so write the difference rather than a briefing.

tools.doc:
Run a copy of yourself, in parallel, on something you will not do yourself.

The copy has your model, your tools and a private copy of your whole conversation, so `prompt` is the *difference* rather than a briefing — everything you have worked out is already there.

Its handle comes back immediately, but the copy itself starts once this turn's tool results are recorded (the conversation it inherits has to be a complete one), so `wait_for_subagents` can only collect it on a later turn — do not wait on it in the program that made it.

Raises `ToolError`: `:limit_exceeded` at the delegation depth cap.

helpers.name: read_text_file

signatures.signature: read_text_file(path, offset: nil, limit: nil) -> String

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file to read. Relative to your workspace, or absolute.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.doc: The 1-based line to start at. Honoured only under a capped read policy.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.doc: How many lines to return from `offset`. Honoured only under a capped read policy.

helpers.doc:
Read a text file and return its contents directly — `fs.read_file` without the narrowing, for the common case.

Takes the same `offset`/`limit` window arguments.

Raises `ToolError`: `:invalid_argument` when the path names a picture; use `fs.read_file` to inspect those.

types.name: ToolError
types.declaration:
class ToolError < StandardError
  attr_reader tool: String
  attr_reader code: Symbol
end
types.doc:
A gg call that failed.

Raised by every function on every API object. Rescue it where a failure is expected and branch on `code`; let it propagate where it is not, and gg reports which call failed and on which line of your program. A handler reads `rescue ToolError => failure` and then `if failure.code == ToolErrorCode::CONFLICT`.

It is a `StandardError`, so a bare `rescue => failure` catches it too — which is what a Ruby programmer expects of anything a library raises.

members.name: tool
members.doc: The gg call that failed (`read_file`, `spawn_subagent`, …). It is gg's own name for the capability, which is stable across every language a program may be written in.

members.name: code
members.doc: The failure class, so a handler branches on a value rather than on prose.

types.name: ToolErrorCode
types.declaration:
module ToolErrorCode
  INVALID_ARGUMENT: :invalid_argument
  NOT_FOUND: :not_found
  CONFLICT: :conflict
  REFUSED: :refused
  UNAVAILABLE: :unavailable
  LIMIT_EXCEEDED: :limit_exceeded
  IO_ERROR: :io_error
  OTHER: :other
end
types.doc: Why a call failed — the `code` on a raised `ToolError`, and the value a handler branches on instead of matching on prose. Every one of them is a Symbol, so the constants below and the symbol literals a program writes (`:not_found`) are the same value.

members.name: INVALID_ARGUMENT
members.doc: The arguments were malformed, ill-typed, or out of range — including a path that is absolute or climbs out of the workspace, and an agent name this run does not declare.

members.name: NOT_FOUND
members.doc: The named file, skill, memory, task, epic, issue, subagent, stored program, or documentation entry does not exist.

members.name: CONFLICT
members.doc: Well-formed, but in conflict with the current state: an ambiguous edit, a dependency cycle, a duplicate id, a subagent that already returned.

members.name: REFUSED
members.doc: gg refused the call on a rule about your state: a compaction in flight that this call is not the one it asked for, a memory call while your memories are read-only, a second ending or hand-over in a turn that already declared one, or a hook that blocked it. A ceiling you ran into is `:limit_exceeded`, not this.

members.name: UNAVAILABLE
members.doc: The call exists but this run's capability set does not offer it. Your program can see every function this SDK has; the ones the run withheld are refused here, by gg, rather than hidden.

members.name: LIMIT_EXCEEDED
members.doc: A gg-side ceiling was hit: a shell timeout, a store cap, the delegation depth cap, one of the view caps this program spends, or the run's wall-clock budget.

members.name: IO_ERROR
members.doc: The underlying I/O or process failed.

members.name: OTHER
members.doc: The failure was not classified. Reserved for outcomes raised outside a tool implementation (gg's own bridge and degradation paths); nothing you call produces it.

types.name: Unchanged
types.declaration:
module Unchanged
  UNCHANGED: :unchanged
end
types.doc:
The "leave this field exactly as it is" value, and the default of every patch argument that can also be *cleared*.

A field a patch may clear has three states rather than two, and Ruby already spells "absent" as `nil` — which here is the request to clear it. So the third state gets a name of its own: leave the argument out (or pass `UNCHANGED`) to keep what is there, pass `nil` to empty it, pass a string to replace it. A field with no clear state is an ordinary `nil` default, where `nil` simply means you are not changing it.

members.name: UNCHANGED
members.doc: Leave the field exactly as it is. It is bound at the top level as well, so a program writes `UNCHANGED` rather than `Unchanged::UNCHANGED`.

types.name: TurnRange
types.declaration: type TurnRange = Range
types.doc:
An inclusive span of turn numbers, the unit `context.archive_thread` moves out of your window — and Ruby's own `Range`, because that is what a span of integers is in this language.

The numbers are the ones on the header of every result you are given, so `4..19` means exactly the turns you can see numbered 4 through 19, both ends included. An exclusive range (`4...20`) means the same thing and is read the same way.
